relearning.title: Read: covalent bonds and naming
relearning.description: A short reading with the shared-pizza analogy, worked examples and quick checks.

body.text:
**I can explain how covalent bonds form and name covalent compounds.**

**Think of splitting a pizza.** Nobody gives the pizza away; you both eat from it. A **covalent bond** works the same way. Two **nonmetal** atoms both need more electrons, and neither will give any up, so they **share**.

**How it forms.** Each atom puts in one electron to make a **shared pair**. The shared pair counts toward the outer level of **both** atoms. That is how both can reach a full outer level: 8 for most atoms, 2 for hydrogen. No electrons are given away, so **no ions form**. A group of atoms joined by covalent bonds is a **molecule**.

**How many bonds?** An atom shares as many electrons as it needs to reach 8. Hydrogen needs 1 more, so it makes 1 bond. Oxygen (6 valence electrons) needs 2 more, so it makes 2 bonds. Nitrogen (5) makes 3. Carbon (4) makes 4.

**Worked example:** water. Oxygen needs 2 more electrons. Each hydrogen needs 1 more. Oxygen shares one pair with each of two hydrogens: **H₂O**. Now oxygen counts 8 and each hydrogen counts 2.

checks.prompt: Two chlorine atoms bond to make Cl₂. What happens to their electrons?

options.text: One chlorine transfers an electron to the other
The two atoms share a pair of electrons

checks.explanation: Chlorine is a nonmetal, and two nonmetals share. One shared pair lets both chlorines count 8. Picking transfer is the common mistake; transfer needs a metal.

checks.prompt: Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons. How many covalent bonds does it make to reach 8? Type a number.
checks.explanation: 8 − 5 = 3, so nitrogen shares 3 more electrons and makes 3 bonds, as in NH₃. Answering 5 (the number it already has) is the common mistake.

sections.title: Double and triple bonds, and names

body.text:
**Single, double, triple.** A **single bond** is 1 shared pair (2 electrons). A **double bond** is 2 shared pairs (4 electrons). A **triple bond** is 3 shared pairs (6 electrons).

**Worked example 2:** O₂. Each oxygen needs 2 more electrons, so the two atoms share 2 pairs: a double bond. In N₂, each nitrogen needs 3 more, so they share 3 pairs: a triple bond.

**Naming covalent compounds.** Use **prefixes** to count the atoms: mono 1, di 2, tri 3, tetra 4, penta 5, hexa 6, hepta 7, octa 8, nona 9, deca 10.

**Rule 1.** The **first element skips mono**. CO₂ is carbon dioxide, not monocarbon dioxide.

**Rule 2.** The **second element always gets a prefix** and an **-ide** ending. CO is carbon monoxide.

**Rule 3.** Drop the extra o or a before oxide: monoxide, tetroxide, pentoxide.

**No criss-cross and no reducing.** The prefixes are the subscripts. N₂O₄ stays N₂O₄: dinitrogen tetroxide.

**Worked example 3:** N₂O₅. Both are nonmetals, so use prefixes. 2 nitrogens → dinitrogen. 5 oxygens → pentoxide. Name: **dinitrogen pentoxide**. Going the other way, sulfur trioxide is 1 sulfur and 3 oxygens: **SO₃**.

**Watch out for:** saying electrons are transferred, saying the atoms become ions, counting a single bond as 1 electron instead of 2, putting mono on the first element, leaving out the prefixes ("phosphorus chloride"), reducing a covalent formula, and using Roman numerals on nonmetals.

checks.prompt: Nitrogen gas, N₂, has a triple bond. How many electrons are shared in it?
checks.explanation: A triple bond is 3 shared pairs, and each pair is 2 electrons: 3 × 2 = 6. Answering 3 counts pairs instead of electrons, which is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: What is the correct name of PCl₃?
checks.explanation: One phosphorus (the first element skips mono) and three chlorines (tri-): phosphorus trichloride. Leaving out the prefix is the common mistake.

sections.shortAnswer: Explain why O₂ has a double bond but N₂ has a triple bond. Use the number of valence electrons each atom has.

relearning.title: Do: flip the covalent rules, then build a molecule step by step
relearning.description: Flashcards with a 3-question self-quiz, then one molecule worked from bond to formula to name.

cards.back: Two nonmetal atoms share valence electrons, like splitting a pizza.
2 electrons that count toward the outer level of both atoms.
A group of atoms joined by covalent bonds, like H₂O. No ions form.
As many as the atom needs to reach 8. H makes 1, O makes 2, N makes 3, C makes 4.
Prefixes count the atoms. The first element skips mono. The second always gets a prefix and ends in -ide.

checks.prompt: Which pair of atoms would form a covalent bond?
checks.explanation: Carbon and oxygen are both nonmetals, so they share electrons. The other pairs have a metal, which transfers electrons instead. Missing the metal is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: How many electrons are shared in a double bond?
checks.explanation: A double bond is 2 shared pairs, and each pair is 2 electrons: 4. Answering 2 counts the pairs instead of the electrons, which is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: What is the correct name of CO?
checks.explanation: The first element skips mono, but the second element always gets a prefix: carbon monoxide. Leaving mono off oxide is the common mistake.

body.problem: Nitrogen bonds with hydrogen. Explain how the bonds form, then write the formula. Then name N₂O₃.

steps.text: Transfer or share? Nitrogen and hydrogen are both nonmetals, so they share electrons. This is covalent.
What does each atom need? Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons and needs 3 more to reach 8. Hydrogen has 1 and needs 1 more to reach 2.
Share. Nitrogen makes one shared pair with each of 3 hydrogens. Formula: NH₃, with three single bonds.
Check. Nitrogen counts its 5 plus 3 shared = 8. Each hydrogen counts 2. Shared electrons in all: 3 bonds × 2 = 6.
Now a name: N₂O₃. Two nonmetals, so use prefixes. 2 nitrogens → dinitrogen. 3 oxygens → trioxide. Name: dinitrogen trioxide.

checks.prompt: Your turn: carbon has 4 valence electrons. How many hydrogen atoms does one carbon atom bond with?
checks.explanation: Carbon needs 4 more electrons to reach 8, and each hydrogen shares 1, so it bonds with 4 hydrogens: CH₄. Answering 8 confuses the goal with the number needed.

checks.prompt: Your turn: what is the correct name of SF₆?
checks.explanation: One sulfur (no mono on the first element) and six fluorines (hexa-): sulfur hexafluoride. Leaving out the prefix is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Carbon and oxygen are both nonmetals. What is the correct name of CO?
checks.explanation: Covalent, so use prefixes. The first element gets a prefix except mono, so just carbon. The second element always gets a prefix and -ide: monoxide. Answer: carbon monoxide.

checks.prompt: Sulfur and oxygen are both nonmetals. Complete the name of SO₃: sulfur ___
checks.explanation: Covalent, so use prefixes. One sulfur gets no prefix (no mono on the first element). Three oxygens → tri + oxide = trioxide. Answer: sulfur trioxide.
